title: Beginner tips on prompting decent game music (for free)
author: Comet7777
selftext:
AI game music doesn't have to suck. Take it from someone who is a certified VGM geek. If you don't know what that abbreviation is, you have much nerdom to discover!  
  
I break down my exact prompt line by line: the style lock, tempo and BPM, major vs minor keys, picking instruments, building and resolving tension, making a track loop seamlessly, and theme and variation across a whole soundtrack. I also cover where AI music still struggles and why your soundtrack needs one consistent style (and the rare times breaking it works).  
  
The actual prompt for the song I was shooting for: "Somber orchestral-electronic overworld theme for a gritty 16-bit sci-fi JRPG, inspired by SNES-era soundtracks (Chrono Trigger "Corridors of Time" mood, Final Fantasy VI "Terra" melancholy, Xenogears). Slow tempo around 72 BPM, in a minor key. Opens with a lonely solo melody on a soft synth flute over a low string pad and distant wind. A warm but weary French horn takes the second phrase. Light military snare brushes and a slow timpani pulse enter in the middle section, then a short hopeful lift on strings before it settles back into melancholy. Subtle analog synth arpeggio underneath for a faint futuristic edge. Feeling: stranded on an unknown, overcast frontier world, grief for a lost ship and lost friends, quiet resolve to keep walking. Retro 16-bit timbre with warm reverb, no vocals, no drums dominating, loops seamlessly, [2:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-9ejmEtYPPg&t=120s)–[2:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-9ejmEtYPPg&t=150s) long."

**Of course this isn't perfect**, nothing with AI will ever be - but it's a decent starting point. AI music generation (at least the cheaper options) is noticeably less sophisticated than other parts of genAI, so I'll look forward to see how this evolves.
